one_liner: LLVM-based JIT for numeric Python: @njit-compiled NumPy loops run 1.4x to 450x faster than CPython 3.12 in pyccel-benchmarks.
what_it_does: Numba compiles decorated Python functions (@njit / @jit, nopython mode by default since 0.59) to machine code on first call, specialised to the argument types. It accepts a large numeric subset of Python and NumPy, plus @jitclass for simple typed classes, @vectorize ufuncs, C callbacks and parallel=True loop parallelisation. The API is a decorator on existing functions, so the source stays Python; code outside the supported subset fails to compile rather than running slowly.
how_it_is_fast: Type inference over Python bytecode turns dynamically typed loops into statically typed LLVM IR (via llvmlite), so element accesses on NumPy arrays become native loads and stores with no boxing or interpreter dispatch. LLVM then optimises and, with fastmath=True, may reassociate floating-point reductions so they vectorise (the docs' sqrt-sum example drops from 35.2 ms to 17.8 ms). Compiled functions can release the GIL (nogil=True) and parallel=True splits supported loops across a threading layer (TBB, OpenMP or workqueue).
when_to_use: Hot scalar loops over NumPy arrays that cannot be expressed as whole-array NumPy calls: graph algorithms, ODE time stepping, stencils written element by element (Poisson 451x, Bellman-Ford 421x, Dijkstra 279x over CPython in the benchmark, derived from page data).

Functions that run long enough (docs: above about 10 us per call) to amortise dispatch, and processes that live long enough to amortise 0.3 to 6.8 CPU seconds of first-call compilation per kernel, or that can use cache=True.

Pure-Python projects that want a pip-installable accelerator without a C/C++ build step: wheels exist for CPython 3.10 to 3.15 (including free-threaded 3.14t) on Linux x86-64 and aarch64, Windows x64/arm64 and macOS arm64.
Multithreaded numeric code where nogil=True or parallel=True lets compiled kernels run on several cores without the GIL.
when_not_to_use: Code that is already vectorised NumPy: in the same benchmark the whole-array FD Laplace kernel is only 1.4x faster than CPython, and Numba's own docs show an @njit-decorated NumPy expression running at NumPy speed (0.659 s vs 0.581 s without Numba).
Short-lived scripts or functions under about 10 us: JIT compilation (0.33 to 6.75 CPU s per kernel here) and call dispatch dominate; the FAQ says to leave such functions alone.

When the last 2x to 8x matters: on the finite-difference kernels Numba trails pythran_gnu by 4.6x to 8.4x, and on Midpoint Fixed it is 297 ms vs 7.24 ms for pyccel_intel_c (derived from page data); ahead-of-time translators win there.
Object-heavy Python (classes beyond @jitclass, async, dict/set comprehensions, **kwargs, re-raised exceptions): unsupported in nopython mode.
Calling from C++ without a Python runtime: the numba.pycc ahead-of-time path is deprecated.

integration.dependencies: llvmlite (0.50.x for Numba 0.68.0, bundles LLVM), NumPy >=1.22,<2.6; optional TBB or OpenMP for parallel=True
integration.min_toolchain: CPython 3.10+ (0.68.0 wheels for 3.10 to 3.15 and 3.14t); no compiler needed at install time
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64, Windows 10+ x64 (arm64 wheels for 3.12+), macOS 11+ arm64; parallel=True only on 64-bit; NVIDIA GPUs of compute capability 5.0+ listed as a supported target
integration.thread_safety: Compiled functions may run concurrently when nogil=True, with the usual race caveats left to the user; for parallel=True the 'default' threading layer gives no specific safety guarantee, 'threadsafe'/'forksafe'/'safe' (TBB) can be requested.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — add @njit to existing functions; only the supported Python/NumPy subset compiles, and the first call per type signature pays compilation

gotchas: Harness note: the record's 'scalar loops' description is not true for every kernel. FD Laplace is whole-array NumPy slicing in both the CPython and Numba files (only the decorator differs), which is why it gains only 1.4x; the ODE kernels (Euler, midpoint, RK4) apply NumPy slice operations to 1-element rows a million times, a CPython worst case that inflates those ratios. The harness never compares outputs across accelerators, and every compiled column uses fast-math (Numba fastmath=True; pyccel and pythran -O3 -march=native -ffast-math).

fastmath=True, used in all benchmark kernels, changes IEEE semantics: the docs show (x - y) + y with y = inf returning 0.0 instead of nan. Global variables are frozen as compile-time constants, and KeyboardInterrupt is ignored until compiled code returns.
cache=True stores compiled code as pickles; loading a malicious cache file executes arbitrary code, so the cache directory must be trusted.

The measured 0.66.0 and the current 0.68.0 carry an open 1D array-indexing regression (issue #10851, opened 2026-09-22: reads about 1.64x and writes about 1.67x slower than 0.65 on arrays above about 5000 elements, now slower than plain NumPy), milestoned for 0.68.1; 55 open performance-labelled issues include slow non-contiguous sum (#9819) and a jitclass slowdown since 0.62 (#10451).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Numba over the CPython copy-and-patch JIT (7-8% geomean) or Cinder (1.5-4x) when the hot code is numeric loops over NumPy arrays, where Numba gains one to two orders of magnitude; pick it over Hana Jit, PPy or DIO-JIT when maturity matters, since those smaller JITs claim wins over Numba on a few microbenchmarks but lack its 11.2k-star user base, wheels for every current CPython and Anaconda-sponsored maintenance.
verified_claims_summary: In the Pyccel developers' pyccel-benchmarks dev-branch run (2026-08-03, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, CPU not recorded), Numba 0.66.0 with llvmlite 0.48.0 and @njit(fastmath=True) beat interpreted CPython 3.12 on all 13 kernels, from 1.4x on the vectorised FD Laplace to 451x on FD Poisson (geometric mean about 115x, derived from page data), timed with python -m timeit best of 5 after timeit's autorange call absorbed the JIT compilation.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-05, 0.68.0 on PyPI 2026-09-30), BSD-2-Clause and pip/conda installable, so copyable as a dependency; the benchmark is independent (B) but from a single shared-VM run with no CPU model and no output validation.
